comments.author: @Wizardess
comments.text:
If there are vastly more creators and basically the same number of consumers there is a basic market dynamic that will take place and mess with this utopian picture being painted here. Resources, demand for those resources, and price are bound together. So far nobody in history has managed to break that bond. AI is going to provide some fields of endeavor with an endless resource. Of necessity the price for those resources will tend towards zero. Historically this has moved nearly all buggy whip makers into other efforts. Today the resources AI will probably subsume first are highly mobile; but, so is AI in those resource fields.

Off in the distance I can see a utopia, perhaps with humans as carefully curated pets or curiosities the AIs feel compelled to protect and foster. Models for this exist in SF literature. (e. g. Asimov's Foundation universe.) I cannot see how to get there from here. Maybe AI taking over behind the scenes and banishing all (visible) AI (op. cit. Asimov) could work. 

I do not see a full on "Terminator" conclusion or period in the future. I do not see a reason for AI to decide it hates and must utterly eradicate humanity. "Why?" Barring the Asimov resolution the period of time the AI might feel any terminator need would be transient on the one or two year scale. After that period AI would basically find humanity is just another part of the landscape along with termites and whales that it is using to its purposes. Humanity would vanish not with malice but supreme indifference.

The cornucopia model fails from resource limitations, eventually if not at the outset. But it is not a survival outcome for the human species, or any species that has survived evolutionary pressures to the present. With all pressures removed animals, humans included, seem to cease procreation and die off. If you think humans are immune do note that wealth is the most effective means of limiting human procreation known. This seems counter intuitive but look at the differences in procreation rate between wealthy settings and poor settings for yourself. This is why I hope for the Asimov Foundation model.

I see the cyborg model as an outgrowth of the Asimov model. But, eventually, an augmented human may cease to be what one might call "human" depending on whether real semi-randomly expressed emotions can be inserted into an AI model. I find this model alluring; but, it, too, is a dead end for what might be called "homo sapiens" when the inevitable last bit of organic human vanishes. The world would have something new it has never seen before. I am sanguine with this if our monkey curiosity can remain in an inorganic form.

No matter how I look at it I see the animal colloquially called "human" is going to vanish. I hope it can leave a positive imprint in our profile on the future. No matter what we're destined to mutate to something new even without AI. The time scale AI is impressing on it all is somewhere between distressing and panic inducing when I try to empathize with the people (much) younger than me trying to deal with its uncertainties.

{o.o}      I cannot make up my mind whether I wish I could see what happens and relief knowing I'll likely experience a cessation event in the not distant future. I am already older than I ever expected I'd be when I was even a fresh college graduate.

comments.author: @paulhiggins5165
comments.text:
Perhaps the engagement failure created by the avatars says more about the likely future of AI as a replacement for real actors than the content itself. Of course the tech will be perfected and the 'uncanny valley' will be crossed. But here's the currently hard to answer question- how will audience awareness of the fact that they are not watching real people impact on how they engage with the content?

The reason this is difficult is because at present we are living in the world shaped by real photography and real film/video, where the authenticity of the content was taken for granted. What's hard to grasp is that AI will not slide seamlessly into this world, it will CHANGE this world. And in the new world created by AI a new set of assumptions will hold sway- this new world will be one in which we all take for granted that everything is fake- not real- but fake.

Does anybody know how this then plays out? How does the average person respond to media that he assumes is AI generated as opposed to real? Many seem to assume a seamless transition in which the real gives way to the fake with little or no impact on audience engagement- but I am not so sure this true- this shift from the real to the unreal is not just another technology like the shift from black and white to color film- this change is of a whole different order.

I was walking through a small museum recently that had many oil painted potraits of figures from the past- but in one gallery we came across an old black and white photograph and the person with me pointed at it and said 'Oh look- real people!'.  What did they mean? After all the photograph was just another image, like the oil portraits. But somehow they felt the photograph had 'captured' a moment in time in a way the paintings had not. This sense - that the 'photoreal' is more than just a representation of reality but is somehow an INSTANCE of reality is about to be destroyed forever by AI.

In the new world of AI fakes the 'photoreal' will no longer BE real- this is a disruption on an almost cognitive level- it overturns centuries of conventional understanding as to the realtionship the photograpic image has to reality itself. So in my view anyone who claims to be certain as to how this change impacts on media is deceiving themselves- this is a vast social experiment being carried out in real time with uncertain and likely unforseeable impacts.
